title: AI-assisted optimization of warm forging using real-time MES sensor data
abstract: Abstract The increasing demand for high functionality and dimensional precision in manufacturing has intensified the need for advanced production technologies for corrosion-resistant stainless-steel fasteners. Conventional nut production relies largely on cold forging or machining; however, stainless steels such as SUS304 and SUS316 exhibit low formability at room temperature, resulting in machining-dependent processes with high cost and low material yield. To address these limitations, this study develops an intelligent warm-forging process system capable of producing stainless-steel nuts with improved precision and process stability, based on real-time multi-sensor data and AI modeling. Key process variables—including Material Heating Temperature, Wedge Stroke, Material Feed Length, Die Temperature, Product Temperature, Forming Force, and dimensional responses such as Head Outer Diameter, Body Outer Diameter, Product Height—were continuously collected from an operating production line. Statistical analysis, correlation analysis, causal inference, and machine-learning models were applied to quantify the effects of these variables on dimensional variation and defect rates. The resulting models were integrated into a smart-manufacturing execution system (MES) that supports real-time monitoring, AI-based defect prediction, and parameter guidance. A formal causal analysis using directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) and the DoWhy framework was conducted to distinguish causal from correlational relationships among process variables. Model generalization was assessed through temporally ordered train–test splitting and 5-fold cross-validation, and a systematic error-source analysis was performed to identify unmeasured confounders limiting dimensional prediction performance. The proposed framework demonstrates the feasibility of AI-assisted warm forging, enabling more consistent product quality, reduced deviation, and enhanced process reliability, thereby contributing to the digital transformation of Korea’s core manufacturing sectors.
journal: The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The increasing demand for high functionality, enhanced durability, and dimensional precision across manufacturing industries has intensified the need for advanced production technologies for precision components. Corrosion-resistant stainless-steel nuts, widely used in automotive, construction, and machinery applications, require manufacturing processes that simultaneously ensure high product quality and efficient productivity. Traditionally, nut manufacturing has relied on cold forging or machining. However, corrosion-resistant stainless steels such as SUS304 and SUS316 exhibit low formability at room temperature, causing manufacturers to depend predominantly on machining processes. This reliance results in high production costs, long processing times, and low material yield.

To address these industrial challenges, Moornmo Co., Ltd. initiated a research program aimed at developing an intelligent warm-forging process system capable of producing corrosion-resistant stainless-steel nuts with improved economic efficiency and dimensional precision. Warm forging offers a favorable balance between hot and cold forging: it requires less energy than hot forging while enabling simpler forming sequences and higher accuracy than cold forging. Despite these advantages, the widespread industrial adoption of warm forging has been hindered by the complexity of process control—particularly in regulating Material Heating Temperature (MHT) and Die Temperature (DT), optimizing lubrication conditions, securing sufficient die life, and maintaining stable forming loads.

In precision warm forging, even subtle fluctuations in process parameters—such as MHT, Wedge Stroke (WS), and Material Feed Length (MFL)—can critically influence the resulting product quality. Although previous studies have examined certain process parameters and their qualitative effects on forging outcomes, a systematic and data-driven approach integrating real-time sensing, quantitative analysis, and artificial intelligence (AI) modeling remains insufficiently explored for warm forging of corrosion-resistant components. This limitation restricts the industry’s transition from traditional experience-based operation to predictive and autonomous process control.

To overcome these limitations, the present research conducted by Moornmo aims to establish a data-centric methodology for understanding and optimizing the warm-forging process of stainless-steel nuts. The specific objectives of this study are to: Quantify the influence of Material Heating Temperature (MHT) in the heating unit on product characteristics and dimensional variation. Analyze the relationship between WS, Forming Force (FF), and resultant product geometry. Evaluate the combined effects of MFL and MHT on dimensional accuracy and product quality. To achieve these objectives, major process parameters were measured in real time and systematically analyzed using statistical and AI-based methods. Correlations and causal relationships between process conditions and quality outcomes were identified, and the derived insights were used to design an AI feedback system capable of adaptively controlling forming conditions to minimize dimensional deviations and reduce defect rates. The broader significance of this research lies in demonstrating the feasibility and industrial applicability of an intelligent warm-forging control system for high-precision stainless-steel components. The proposed approach is expected to enhance product reliability, stabilize process variability, and contribute to establishing a smart-manufacturing-based production framework within the forging industry. Ultimately, this work supports the digital transformation of Korea’s root manufacturing sectors and advances global competitiveness in precision forming technologies.

sections.heading: Related works
paragraphs: This section reviews the state of the art along the four axes on which the present study builds: (i) warm forging of stainless steel and its process characteristics, (ii) the influence of individual process variables on dimensional quality, (iii) data-driven and AI-assisted forging optimisation, and (iv) causal inference and explainability for manufacturing process data. Throughout, emphasis is placed on work published in the last five years, and on identifying the specific gap—the fusion of continuous, multi-sensor industrial production data with interpretable and causally-validated modelling for warm forging—that this paper addresses.

sections.heading: Warm forging of stainless steel and process characteristics
paragraphs: Warm forging occupies an intermediate position between cold and hot forging and is valued for combining relatively low forming loads with good dimensional precision and reduced work hardening, which makes it attractive for low-formability materials such as austenitic stainless steels [ 1 ]. The central difficulty is that the mechanical response of these steels is strongly coupled to temperature and strain rate. Zheng et al. [ 2 ] characterised the flow behaviour of SUS304 across a wide range of forming temperatures and strain rates, showing that flow stress falls with increasing temperature but exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on strain rate at lower temperatures, driven by deformation-induced martensitic transformation. This temperature and rate sensitivity is precisely what makes material heating temperature (MHT) a first-order process variable, and it explains why nominally small heating fluctuations can produce disproportionate changes in forming load and filling behaviour.

This temperature and rate dependence is a general feature of austenitic stainless steels: Radionova et al. [ 3 ] characterised the hot-deformation behaviour of AISI 321, showing that flow stress rises with decreasing temperature and increasing strain rate and that a Zener–Hollomon (hyperbolic-sine) constitutive law, together with dynamic recrystallisation, is needed to describe it. Because the underlying constitutive response is thus strongly nonlinear, recent work has increasingly modelled it with data-driven methods. Song [ 4 ] showed that a random-forest model [ 5 ] reproduces the flow stress of 304 stainless steel in the 700–900 °C regime more accurately than a classical Arrhenius-type constitutive equation, and in a companion study [ 6 ] reached the same conclusion for 316L, where neural-network and support-vector-regression models outperformed the Arrhenius formulation. These results are directly relevant to the present work in two ways: they confirm that tree- and kernel-based learners are well suited to the thermo-mechanical response of the SUS304/SUS316 family, and they motivate the choice of Random Forest [ 5 ] as the primary regressor here.

The consequences of this temperature sensitivity for a real forged part were quantified by Byun et al. [ 7 ], who characterised the flow stress of SUS304 from room temperature to 400 °C and embedded it in a non-isothermal elasto-thermo-viscoplastic finite-element analysis of automatic multi-stage cold forging of an SUS304 ball-stud. By comparing isothermal and non-isothermal analyses they showed that the temperature rise from viscous heating—up to 90% of the deformation energy is dissipated as heat—materially changes the predicted forming load, die stress and die wear, and hence the dimensional accuracy after ejection. This is strong evidence that, even for a nominally “cold” or warm SUS304 forging, the thermal state and the resulting die wear are first-order determinants of dimensional outcome; the present study treats exactly these quantities as partially observed variables and unmeasured confounders. The difficulty of observing that thermal state on a real line was underscored by Hawryluk et al. [ 8 ], who, analysing multi-stage forging of stainless-steel valve and slender bolt-type forgings, found large discrepancies between induction-heater set-points and the actual billet-surface temperatures measured by thermal imaging, with the resulting thermal non-uniformity leading directly to localised defects and premature tool failure. This is precisely the kind of set-point-versus-actual gap that limits how much of the dimensional variance the logged MHT and DT signals can explain in the present dataset.

A recurring theme is that the thermal state actually governing deformation is difficult to observe. Plogmeyer et al. [ 9 ] embedded thin-film sensors directly in the die during warm forging and showed that transient die-surface temperature gradients at the tool–workpiece interface are far steeper than bulk thermocouple readings indicate. This finding underpins a key assumption of the present study: die temperature (DT) as logged by line sensors is a noisy proxy for the thermally relevant quantity, and this measurement gap must be treated explicitly rather than ignored.

sections.heading: Process variables, dimensional accuracy and tool state
paragraphs: A large body of forging research examines how individual process parameters govern die filling and dimensional outcome, most often through finite-element (FE) simulation. Okamoto et al. [ 10 ] proposed an optimisation-support method for cold and warm forging dies of non-axisymmetrical products, demonstrating via FE analysis that die geometry strongly shapes material flow and dimensional accuracy, while Wang et al. [ 11 ] used multi-objective optimisation of radial-forging die surface parameters to improve dimensional uniformity. Both establish die design as a lever for accuracy, but both are evaluated in simulation rather than against production-line measurement.

At the process-design level, Lee et al. [ 12 ] showed for small automotive solenoid-valve parts that partitioning forming into a well-designed sequence of stages, with preforms tuned to induce uniform plastic deformation, is what secures dimensional accuracy on outer diameter and length—underlining that stroke and feed allocation across stages, not a single lumped parameter, governs the final geometry. Jo et al. [ 13 ] reached a compatible conclusion for a long one-body input shaft, where FEA-guided multi-stage cold forging produced a defect-free part with markedly better strength and material-recovery than machining, again showing that per-stage deformation allocation is decisive. This motivates the present study’s explicit treatment of wedge stroke (WS) and material feed length (MFL) as distinct, separately controllable variables.

Tool state enters this picture not only through wear but through fatigue. Joun et al. [ 14 ] proposed a general fatigue-limit diagram to predict the high-cycle fatigue life of cold-forging dies, showing that die life is governed by the interaction of mean stress and stress amplitude under the high-yield, low-ductility conditions typical of forging tooling. Because die-life exhaustion progressively alters cavity geometry, it is a further mechanism—beyond abrasive wear—by which unmeasured tool state feeds into dimensional drift, reinforcing the treatment of die condition as a latent confounder in this work.

Complementing the design-side literature, a series of industrial case studies from Hawryluk and co-workers highlights that realised dimensional accuracy is dominated by the evolving state of the tooling. In a multi-impression hot hydraulic hammer line, they documented that die-cavity wear, material-to-tool adhesion and thermal cycling jointly degrade repeatability over a production run, and that these degradation modes are difficult to separate from batch- or operator-level variation using aggregate logs [ 15 ]. Redesigning die geometry to eliminate a secondary flange-welding operation measurably improved consistency in conveyor-driver forgings [ 16 ], reinforcing that tool design and wear state—rather than nominal parameter settings alone—are frequently the dominant, and largely unmeasured, drivers of dimensional outcome. The systematic review of tool-durability methods by Turek and Cieślik [ 17 ] reaches a compatible conclusion, identifying die wear, thermal fatigue and lubrication breakdown as the primary failure mechanisms affecting dimensional repeatability. These observations directly motivate the present study’s treatment of die wear and lubrication state as explicit unmeasured confounders in the causal analysis of Section  4.7 , and its introduction of a cumulative-production-count proxy for wear (Section  4.6 ).

On the measurement side, dimensional feedback itself has become denser and more automated. Hawryluk et al. [ 18 ] developed an integrated machine-vision system for shape- and dimensional-accuracy inspection of valve forgings with accuracy sufficient to replace manual coordinate-measuring-machine sampling. Such systems show that high-rate dimensional feedback is now practical, but they have so far been deployed as standalone downstream inspection rather than fused with upstream process data for prediction or causal analysis—exactly the integration pursued here. Taken together, the process-variable literature is characterised by two limitations: variables are usually studied in isolation, and the data typically originate from simulation or laboratory trials rather than continuous production operation.

sections.heading: Data-driven and AI-assisted forging optimisation
paragraphs: The digital transformation of metal forming has produced a rapidly growing body of AI-assisted process work, recently surveyed comprehensively by Cao et al. [ 19 ], whose review of artificial intelligence in metal forming maps the field across constitutive modelling, process design, monitoring and control and notes the persistent scarcity of studies grounded in real production data. Two lines of work are especially relevant. Petrik and Bambach [ 20 ] developed DeepForge, combining 1D convolutional networks and gated recurrent units with model predictive control to regulate microstructure in closed-die hot forging; Reinisch et al. [ 21 ] coupled reinforcement learning with fast process models for closed-loop microstructure control in forging and rolling, achieving online adaptation within seconds. Both are important advances in closed-loop AI control, yet both are trained and validated on FE-simulation data and target microstructure rather than the dimensional quality of a production part. Xu et al. [ 22 ] moved closer to the shop floor with an ANN-based decision system for free forging of an engine main shaft that recommended forming parameters reducing dimensional deviation relative to operator baselines; however, the system operated open-loop on a single forging type, without multi-sensor data fusion or any causal validation of its recommendations.

Data-driven prediction of dimensional outcome has itself been demonstrated: Cai et al. [ 23 ] trained machine-learning models to predict the thinning and thickening of hot-stamped parts under partition temperature control, confirming that learners can map process settings to geometric response—but, like the studies above, they did so on finite-element-generated data rather than production measurements. A cross-cutting limitation, emphasised by the systematic review of Presciuttini et al. [ 24 ], is that ML applications on manufacturing IoT data concentrate on maintenance rather than production, rely predominantly on a narrow set of model families, and rarely address interpretability—leaving the causal linkage between process inputs and quality outputs largely unexplored. Digital-twin visions for forming [ 25 ,  26 ] and the broader case for data-intensive smart manufacturing [ 27 ] share the same unrealised premise: their value depends on continuous, trustworthy, interpretable production data that warm forging lines seldom expose. The result is that AI work specifically targeting warm forging—with its tightly coupled thermo-mechanical behaviour requiring simultaneous monitoring of MHT, DT, wedge stroke (WS), material feed length (MFL) and forming force (FF)—remains sparse, and almost none of it operates on real, large-scale, multi-sensor production data.

sections.heading: Causal inference and explainability for process data
paragraphs: The idea that forming quality should be regulated rather than merely inspected has a well-established foundation: the CIRP keynote of Allwood et al. [ 28 ] framed metal forming as a control problem in which product properties degrade from specification because of parameter variation and imperfect process understanding, and argued that closed-loop control is the principled remedy. Realising such control on a warm-forging line, however, requires first identifying which measured variables genuinely drive the controlled outputs—a prerequisite that predictive accuracy alone does not satisfy, since correlations in observational production data are frequently confounded. Two complementary tool families have emerged to close this gap. Post-hoc explainability, and in particular the SHAP framework of Lundberg and Lee [ 29 ], attributes model predictions to individual inputs; comparative studies such as Wang et al. [ 30 ] have since examined when SHAP-based feature ranking is preferable to a model’s built-in importance measures, informing the way SHAP is applied alongside Random Forest here. Senoner et al. [ 31 ] showed in large-scale semiconductor manufacturing that SHAP-based explanations can go beyond interpretation to actively guide process changes that measurably reduce defect rates. Causal inference addresses the complementary question of whether an input is genuinely responsible for an outcome. Yang and Bequette [ 32 ] applied a causal-inference framework to real observational steelmaking data and demonstrated that naively interpreting statistical correlations produced incorrect intervention recommendations, whereas explicit causal modelling correctly identified the parameters warranting control action. General-purpose libraries such as DoWhy [ 33 ] have made the corresponding workflow—graph specification, identification via the backdoor criterion, estimation and refutation—practical for engineering datasets.

The present study is, to our knowledge, the first to bring these two families together for warm forging: SHAP provides physical interpretability of a Random Forest quality model, while DoWhy-based causal inference tests whether the statistically important variables are also causally responsible for dimensional outcomes. This directly follows the logic of Yang and Bequette [ 32 ] and extends the actionable-XAI use case of Senoner et al. [ 31 ] into the forging domain.

sections.heading: Research gap and contribution
paragraphs: Synthesising the above, four gaps persist. First, process variables are predominantly studied in isolation and via simulation, rather than jointly and from production data [ 10 ,  11 ,  13 ]. Second, AI-assisted forging work concentrates on hot or cold forging and on microstructure, with warm-forging dimensional quality on real multi-sensor data largely unaddressed [ 19 ,  20 ,  21 ,  22 – 23 ]. Third, despite growing demand for SUS304/SUS316 precision fasteners, systematic data-driven studies targeting these materials remain limited, and those that exist are predominantly simulation-based [ 2 ,  3 – 4 ,  6 ,  7 ,  12 ]. Fourth, predictive models are rarely paired with interpretability and formal causal validation, so recommended parameter changes cannot be distinguished from confounded correlations [ 24 ,  29 ,  30 ,  31 – 32 ].

Against this backdrop, the present work contributes a study that (1) collects synchronised multi-sensor data (MHT, DT, WS, MFL, FF and dimensional responses HOD, BOD, PH) directly from a commercial warm-forging line for SUS304 nuts, (2) jointly analyses the relationships among these variables rather than one at a time, (3) predicts both defect rates and dimensional outcomes with ML models whose behaviour is made interpretable via SHAP, and (4) applies formal causal inference to separate causal from correlational effects and to reason explicitly about unmeasured confounders such as die wear and lubrication state. Unlike the simulation-based microstructure-control frameworks of Petrik and Bambach [ 20 ] and Reinisch et al. [ 21 ], and unlike the single-part open-loop decision system of Xu et al. [ 22 ], the framework here operates entirely on real production data and is embedded within a manufacturing-execution-system (MES) platform, simultaneously targeting multiple dimensional outcomes and defect rates within one continuous-monitoring pipeline.

sections.heading: Definition of variables
Overall analysis framework
paragraphs: The overall procedure used to analyze the collected data consists of two main streams:  A four-step data analysis procedure A three-step causal analysis procedure The four-step data analysis procedure comprises:  Data collection and preprocessing – multi-sensor acquisition, synchronization, and cleaning (Sections  3.3 – 3.4 ). Data visualization – time-series plots and distribution charts to identify trends and anomalies. Correlation analysis – quantification of relationships among process variables (MHT, DT, WS, MFL, FF) and dimensional outcomes (HOD, BOD, PH, head thickness). Machine learning analysis – AI models trained to predict quality metrics from process conditions. The causal analysis procedure is implemented within Moornmo’s MES service and is used to move beyond pure correlation toward causal interpretation of defect mechanisms. It consists of:  Root-cause analysis using a defect detection model SHAP-based local explainability Causal inference using the DoWhy library [ 33 ], including formal DAG specification, identification via the backdoor criterion, and refutation testing (Section  4.7 ) Defective products detected by the vision inspection system have their associated MHT, WS, MFL, DT, PT, FF, HOD, BOD, PH records fed into an integrated defect detection model within MES. Feature importance metrics identify process variables that contribute most strongly to the defect rate. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis provides local interpretability at the individual-part level, and causal inference verifies whether candidate variables are not only correlated with defects but also have plausible causal effects on defect occurrence.

This combination of procedures enables data-driven identification of the process conditions most responsible for quality variations and supports the design of intelligent control strategies for defect reduction.

sections.heading: Hypothesis formulation
paragraphs: To verify the reliability and internal consistency of the collected data, a set of working hypotheses was established prior to analysis. These hypotheses reflect physically reasonable expectations about how forming conditions affect product dimensions: Hypothesis 1.  As MFL increases, HOD, BOD, head thickness, and PH will increase. Hypothesis 2.  As WS increases, head thickness will decrease, while PH and HOD will increase. Hypothesis 3.  As MHT increases, head thickness and PH will decrease, while HOD will increase. These hypotheses serve as a basis for interpreting the results of the statistical and AI-based analyses presented later.

sections.heading: Data acquisition period and sampling strategy
paragraphs: The data acquisition period spanned from 4 October 2024 to 6 March 2025. During this period, sensors were continuously deployed on the production line to capture multi-modal data: DT and PT were recorded at intervals of approximately 1–2 s. FF (via acoustic measurement) was recorded at intervals of approximately 1 s. Dimensional measurements (HOD, BOD, PH, head thickness) from the vision inspection system were collected at approximately 1 s per part. More than 8,000 parts were produced under varying parameter conditions, providing a dataset suitable for deriving correlations among MHT, WS, MFL, DT, PT, FF and dimensional outcomes.

Sensor data from each measurement point were stored on a local PC and transferred via a C#-based data pipeline to a centralized MySQL database, with data recorded in relational (MySQL), CSV/text (numeric logs), and PNG (waveform/image) formats. The pipeline performed file-based ingestion, data transformation, unit conversion, basic cleaning, RESTful API transmission, and final loading into the central database.

Material feeding and heating occur at the entry station, followed by transfer via conveyor to the forming press where FF is measured. After forming, PT is measured, oil is removed in a degreasing unit, and parts are supplied to a bowl feeder for vision inspection. The total elapsed time from material feeding to vision inspection is approximately two minutes, which is reflected in the data alignment strategy (Section  3.6 ).

sections.heading: Measurement of MHT, MFL, and WS
paragraphs: MHT, MFL, and WS were controlled and recorded through the PLC. Operator-specified setpoints were stored in PLC memory, and the actual heater temperature corresponding to MHT was measured by a sensor on the heater. A PC connected to the PLC ran a C# program that periodically retrieved these values and stored them in a local database before transmission to the central server.

sections.heading: Die temperature measurement (DT)
paragraphs: DT was measured using non-contact temperature sensors directed toward the die surface. Sensors were mounted to maintain constant distance and angle, and temperature was recorded at fixed time intervals, providing time-series data for analyzing thermal stability during operation and evaluating how DT deviations affect product quality.

sections.heading: Product temperature measurement (PT)
paragraphs: PT was initially measured at the lower section of the transfer conveyor after forming and before the degreasing unit. This approach was sensitive to conveyor-speed variation, reducing data reliability. To improve data quality, the measurement point was shifted to the upper section of the conveyor where formed parts accumulate, yielding more stable and consistent PT measurements.

sections.heading: Forming force measurement via acoustic sensing (FF)
paragraphs: FF was not measured directly using a load cell but inferred indirectly using an acoustic sensor attached near the punch region of the former. The sensor recorded sound signals at one-second intervals, capturing approximately 0.57 s of waveform per event. The raw sound signals were normalized based on a reference intensity from the first measurement set. Subsequent data were converted into normalized values and stored as: Time-ordered normalized sound values (text files). An example shown in Fig.  3 . Corresponding waveform images (PNG files). An example shown in Fig.  4 . Fig. 3 An example of the time-ordered normalized sound values for forming force measurement Fig. 4 An example of the waveform image of the time-ordered normalized sound values for forming force measurement

Because of the indirect nature of this method, the acoustic signal is not guaranteed to be strictly proportional to the true forming force and may contain environmental noise. To mitigate this, the minimum, maximum, and average values within each waveform segment were extracted. Preliminary analysis showed that the maximum amplitude was most sensitive to changes in process conditions such as DT and WS, and thus the maximum normalized amplitude was selected as the primary indicator of FF in correlation and regression analyses.

sections.heading: Measurement of dimensional responses using vision inspection
paragraphs: Dimensional outputs—HOD, Left and Right Head Thickness, BOD, and PH—were obtained using an automated vision inspection system. After degreasing, cleaned nuts were aligned in a single row by a bowl feeder and sequentially fed into the vision inspection station. The vision program measured geometrical features and saved results in CSV format on a local PC. A file-watcher mechanism automatically triggered the C# data pipeline to transfer inspection results to the central server.

Based on predefined inspection criteria, each part was classified as pass or fail. The mechanical configuration and the real-time inspection interface are shown in Figs.  5  and  6  respectively. Only parts that satisfied all dimensional tolerances were labeled as “pass” and recorded as conforming products in the main dataset. Fig. 5 The equipment configuration of the vision sorting system installed on the production line is shown. Products are transferred to the inspection station via the feeding mechanism, where a high-resolution industrial camera captures images with controlled illumination to extract surface, dimensional, and geometric features Fig. 6 The real-time inspection interface is presented. The upper screens illustrate examples of acceptable (OK) products in which the measured dimensions and geometric features meet the predefined tolerances. The lower screen shows a defective (NG) case where dimensional deviations exceeding the reference tolerance are detected. The system analyzes the acquired images in real time, automatically classifying products as OK or NG. OK products are conveyed to the loading box, while NG products are discharged through a separate rejection path

sections.heading: Data quality assessment and variable screening
Daily production and defect rate
paragraphs: Several trial runs were conducted to synchronize sensors and tune equipment. After each run, the production results were analyzed and operating conditions adjusted, with the goal of narrowing down optimal parameter ranges for MHT, WS, MFL. Through this iterative tuning, stable operating conditions were established, and data collected after 18 February 2025 were deemed suitable for the main analysis.

Defect rates for dimensional criteria (HOD, BOD, PH, head thickness) under different MHT, WS, MFL combinations were computed. From this analysis, MHT showed a relatively weak effect on defect rate, MFL exhibited modest but limited influence, and WS emerged as the strongest factor affecting defect rates, particularly for HOD and BOD.

sections.heading: Issues related to the vision inspection system
paragraphs: The vision inspection system is critical for precision evaluation and is sensitive to sensor faults and environmental factors. Practical issues included: Residual chips on the glass surface, leading to contamination and artificially increased defect counts. Dust accumulation on the LED light source, causing illumination fluctuation and measurement drift. Due to these issues, some periods of data were deemed unusable. For example, during a specific period height measurements (PH) were unreliable, and punch-pin fracture prevented inner diameter inspection. Consequently, inner diameter was excluded from the final dataset, and only data collected after 18 February 2025 were used for quantitative analysis.

sections.heading: Issues related to the heater
Determination of optimal operating conditions
paragraphs: Because each sensor has a different time lag relative to the production flow, the following approach was used for synchronization: Dimensional data (HOD, BOD, PH, thickness) from the vision system were aligned with process data recorded approximately two minutes earlier. Sensor data were grouped into five-second windows, and average values within each window were computed for MHT, DT, PT, WS, MFL, FF. Among the variables, WS emerged as the most critical factor affecting product quality. When WS is excessive, the material spreads too much, leading to geometric imbalance, folds, or excessive flash. If WS is too small, the die cavity may not be fully filled, resulting in underfill and internal defects.

sections.heading: Time-series visualization of process variables
paragraphs: Time-series plots were generated for 21 February 2025, a representative day with stable operating conditions.

sections.heading: Material Heating Temperature (MHT)
paragraphs: MHT showed in Fig.  7  intermittent discontinuities corresponding to break times or pauses, but overall remained close to setpoints, confirming reliability. Fig. 7 This figure presents a scatter plot illustrating the temporal variation of the Material Heating Temperature (MHT). The MHT generally remained close to its predefined setpoints, although a gradual decrease was observed as time progressed from the initial operation phase. The discontinuities in the data correspond to operator break periods or temporary pauses in machine operation. After the process resumed, the MHT briefly increased and then gradually stabilized. These results indicate that, aside from short interruptions, the MHT remained consistent and reliable throughout the monitoring period

sections.heading: Die Temperature (DT)
paragraphs: DT, as shown in Fig.  8 , gradually increased during continuous operation and cooled during stoppages, reflecting typical thermo–mechanical behavior and confirming its sensitivity to production continuity and cycle time. Fig. 8 This figure illustrates the temporal variation of the Die Temperature (DT) using a scatter-plot representation. During continuous operation, the DT exhibited a gradual increasing trend with a consistent thermal slope, whereas during intermittent process stoppages, the temperature decreased in discrete steps. Upon resumption of operation, the DT again transitioned into an increasing phase. This step-wise thermal profile—comprising repeated cycles of heating, plateau, and cooling—indicates that the die repeatedly re-establishes thermal equilibrium between external heating input and natural cooling. Furthermore, the observation that DT reaches higher temperature levels in later cycles compared to the initial phase suggests a thermal accumulation effect within the die material. This behavior confirms that DT is highly sensitive to production continuity, cycle time, and machine on/off patterns, demonstrating its utility as a key thermo–mechanical indicator reflecting the dynamic conditions of the manufacturing process

sections.heading: Head Outer Diameter (HOD)
paragraphs: The HOD time-series, as shown in Fig.  9 , exhibited increasing variance as production progressed, suggesting dimensional stability may deteriorate over long intervals due to thermal drift, die wear, or MFL variation, justifying later inclusion of DT and WS in correlation and ML analyses. Fig. 9 The scatter plot shows an observable increase in HOD variance as production progresses. The data that lies beyond the minimum and maximum boundaries (dotted lines) are defect products. This trend suggests that external factors such as thermal drift, die wear, or MFL variation may contribute to dimensional instability. These observations motivate the inclusion of additional process variables such as DT and WS in the subsequent correlation and machine-learning analyses

sections.heading: Pairwise relationships among process variables
paragraphs: Scatter plots were generated for several representative days to qualitatively assess relationships. The figures here are not in high quality because those were generated by the MES system of Moornmo. For the purpose of this discussion, however, those are sufficient as we only need to recognise the rough trend while the exact data are fed into ML models for statistical analysis.

sections.heading: MFL vs. HOD
paragraphs: It is shown in Fig.  10  that an increase in MFL generally led to more HOD defects. At approximately 19.0 mm MFL, clusters of HOD values fell below tolerance, implying that excessive MFL may cause unbalanced flow into the head region. Fig. 10 This figure illustrates the correlation between Material Feed Length (MFL) (x-axis) and Head Outer Diameter (HOD) (y-axis) using a scatter-plot representation. While most HOD values remain within the specification limits, a noticeable cluster of measurements near an MFL of approximately 19.0 mm falls below the lower tolerance boundary (LSL). This pattern suggests that excessive MFL may lead to unbalanced material flow into the head region during forming, increasing the likelihood of HOD defects. The trend line indicates that variation in HOD tends to increase as MFL rises, implying a potential negative impact of high MFL values on dimensional stability

sections.heading: MFL vs. PH
paragraphs: Contrary to initial expectations, it is shown in Fig.  11  that PH exhibited a slight decreasing trend as MFL increased, possibly due to redistribution of deformation between head and body regions or compensatory adjustments in WS. Fig. 11 This figure presents the correlation between Material Feed Length (MFL) (x-axis) and final product Height (y-axis) measured under warm forging conditions. The Height values exhibit a very slight decreasing tendency as MFL increases, indicating a weak overall correlation. At lower MFL levels, the Height measurements are tightly clustered, whereas higher MFL values show increased dispersion. This behavior suggests that in warm forging, temperature gradients, material softening, changes in friction conditions, and deformation redistribution exert stronger influence on Height formation than MFL alone

sections.heading: MFL vs. FF
paragraphs: FF (maximum acoustic amplitude) showed a weak but consistent decreasing trend with increasing MFL in Fig.  12 , suggesting that excessive material may act as a buffer altering energy transfer. Fig. 12 This figure illustrates the correlation between Material Feed Length (MFL) (x-axis) and Forming Force (FF) (y-axis), measured as the maximum normalized acoustic amplitude. The FF values exhibit a very slight decreasing tendency as MFL increases, indicating a weak overall correlation. At lower MFL levels, the FF measurements are tightly clustered, whereas higher MFL values show a more dispersed distribution. This behavior suggests that under warm forging conditions, FF is influenced less by MFL alone and more by thermo–mechanical effects, including material softening, temperature gradients, frictional variations, and deformation redistribution during forming

sections.heading: DT vs. PT
paragraphs: The Fig.  13  shows that a strong positive relationship was observed between DT and PT, confirming reliable measurement and expected heat transfer behavior. Fig. 13 This figure illustrates the correlation between Die Temperature (DT) (x-axis) and Product Temperature (PT) (y-axis) using a scatter plot with a fitted trend line. A clear positive linear relationship is observed, with PT consistently increasing as DT rises. In addition, the plot reveals a temperature-dependent variance pattern: PT values are more widely scattered at lower DT levels, while higher DT values show increasingly tighter clustering of PT. This behavior reflects the thermo–mechanical characteristics of warm forging, where higher die temperatures facilitate more stable heat transfer, thereby reducing temperature variability in the product. The distribution pattern further confirms both the reliability of the measurements and the dominant thermal influence of DT on PT

sections.heading: DT vs. FF
paragraphs: The Fig.  14  shows that FF exhibited a slight upward trend with increasing DT, possibly reflecting complex changes in friction, material softening, and contact dynamics. Using maximum amplitude as the representation of FF was crucial to capturing this trend. Fig. 14 This figure presents the scatter plot describing the relationship between Die Temperature (DT) (x-axis) and Forming Force (FF) (y-axis), measured as the maximum normalized acoustic amplitude. The FF values exhibit a slight upward trend with increasing DT, indicating that higher die temperatures are associated with modest increases in forming force. Several low-FF outliers appear, likely corresponding to intermittent underforming events or temporary losses in impact energy. Furthermore, at higher DT levels, the FF values become more tightly clustered, suggesting reduced variability under warm forging conditions. This pattern reflects thermo–mechanical effects such as material softening, frictional changes, and stabilized die–material contact, which can alter the energy transfer during forming. These observations also confirm that representing FF via maximum acoustic amplitude effectively captures the DT–FF relationship

sections.heading: WS vs. HOD
paragraphs: It is shown in Fig.  15  that WS demonstrated a meaningful positive relationship with HOD: larger WS values produced larger HOD, consistent with forging mechanics where deeper penetration promotes lateral flow. Fig. 15 This figure illustrates the correlation between Wedge Stroke (WS) and Head Outer Diameter (HOD) using a scatter plot with a fitted trend line. Although the range of WS variation is narrow, the HOD values exhibit a slight positive trend, increasing as WS becomes larger. This behavior aligns with established forging mechanics, in which a larger wire diameter promotes deeper die penetration and consequently enhances lateral material flow, resulting in larger HOD dimensions. The measurements remain within the specification limits, indicating a stable and consistent influence of WS on HOD

sections.heading: Correlation analysis results
paragraphs: Spearman correlation coefficients were computed to quantify relationships among MHT, DT, MFL, WS, FF and dimensional outcomes and defect rates.

sections.heading: Relationships with defect rates
paragraphs: The Table  1  shows the coefficient of correlation between (the measurements of MFL, maximum WS, DT, MHT, WS and PT) and (the defect rates of HOD, BOD and PH). Two key findings were: MFL showed the strongest positive correlations with defect rates related to HOD, right head thickness, and BOD. WS exhibited the strongest negative correlation with overall defect rates, indicating that sufficiently large WS reduces defects by ensuring full cavity filling. sections.heading: Relationships with dimensional values
Model evaluation strategy
Rationale for model selection
paragraphs: The choice of Linear Regression, Ridge Regression, and Random Forest was guided by three considerations: interpretability, nonlinear capacity, and deployability within the MES environment.

We considered but did not adopt temporally structured models (e.g., LSTM, ARIMA) for the following reasons. The data pipeline aggregates sensor readings into 5-second windows, and the approximately 2-minute lag between forming and vision inspection effectively removes short-term temporal autocorrelation from the aligned dataset. Autocorrelation analysis of the residuals from the Random Forest model confirmed no significant temporal structure (Durbin–Watson statistic: 1.92–2.08 across targets). Recent works using deep sequential architectures, such as Petrik and Bambach [ 20 ], operate on continuous time-series from FE simulations where temporal structure is preserved; in contrast, our aggregated industrial data is better suited to instance-based learners.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) were also considered. However, incorporating physical constraints (e.g., conservation of volume, thermo-mechanical constitutive laws) would require the material’s constitutive parameters under warm forging conditions, which are not readily available for SUS304 at the specific temperature ranges used (150–210 °C). Future work will explore hybrid physics-ML models as these parameters are characterized.

sections.heading: Prediction of dimensional measurements
paragraphs: Three regression models—Linear Regression, Ridge Regression, and Random Forest—were evaluated for predicting dimensional measurements and defect rates from MHT, DT, WS, MFL, FF.

sections.heading: Prediction of dimensional measurements
Prediction of defect rates
Hypothesis testing
Error source analysis for dimensional prediction
Residual time-dependency analysis
paragraphs: Plotting the Random Forest prediction residuals for HOD against chronological production order revealed a systematic drift, with residuals trending negative (under-prediction) in the later portions of each production day. This pattern is consistent with progressive die wear, which gradually enlarges the die cavity and increases HOD beyond model predictions. A similar but weaker drift was observed for PH.

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis via permutation importance
Proxy variable analysis for die wear
Lubrication effects
Thermal drift
paragraphs: DT time-series analysis (Section  4.1 ) showed thermal accumulation effects during continuous operation. Although DT is included as a model input, the single-point surface temperature measurement may not fully capture the 3D temperature distribution within the die, leading to residual thermal effects in the prediction error. Future integration of thermal imaging or multiple temperature sensors at different die locations is expected to improve model performance.

sections.heading: Causal analysis results
paragraphs: To move beyond correlational findings, a formal causal analysis was conducted using the DoWhy library [ 33 ]. The analysis proceeded through four stages: DAG specification, identification, estimation, and refutation.

Summary of key findings

paragraphs: It is instructive to position the present results against the most closely related recent methods, both to clarify the contribution and to interpret the moderate dimensional-prediction accuracy reported above.

sections.heading: Data source: production data versus simulation
Response scope and material
paragraphs: Where recent AI forging studies typically target a single response—microstructure or grain size [ 20 ,  21 ], or the dimensional deviation of one part geometry [ 22 ]—the present framework predicts multiple dimensional outcomes (HOD, BOD, PH) together with defect rates for SUS304 nuts. The choice of Random Forest is itself supported by the recent constitutive-modelling literature for this material family, in which tree- and kernel-based learners outperformed classical Arrhenius formulations for the flow stress of 304 and 316L stainless steel [ 4 ,  6 ]. Our finding that MHT lacks a stable monotonic effect on final dimensions is consistent with the non-monotonic temperature- and rate-dependence of SUS304 flow stress reported by Zheng et al. [ 2 ], and helps explain why heating temperature, although mechanically important, is not the dominant dimensional driver on this line.

sections.heading: From prediction to actionable, validated recommendations
Summary of positioning
paragraphs: Relative to the recent literature, the contribution is therefore not a new learner but an end-to-end pipeline that (i) runs on real multi-sensor production data rather than simulation, (ii) treats multiple dimensional and defect responses jointly, (iii) makes its predictions interpretable, and (iv) subjects its recommendations to formal causal validation—while being explicit, through the error-source and confounder analysis, about the sensing limitations that bound dimensional predictability on an operating line.

sections.heading: System integration and user interface
Conclusion
paragraphs: This study investigated the warm-forging process of corrosion-resistant stainless-steel nuts using a comprehensive methodology that integrates multi-sensor data acquisition of MHT, DT, PT, WS, MFL, FF, dimensional measurement (HOD, BOD, PH, head thickness), statistical analysis, and machine-learning–based prediction.

sections.heading: Scope and boundary conditions
paragraphs: The conclusions of this study are derived from and validated under the following specific conditions:  Product:  M10-size SUS304 stainless-steel hexagonal nuts. Equipment:  A single warm-forging production line with induction heating. Temperature range:  MHT = 150–210 °C; DT = 12–60 °C. WS range:  6.9–7.3 mm. MFL range:  18.9–19.1 mm. The identified dominance of WS as the primary quality driver is expected to generalize to similar fastener geometries with comparable aspect ratios and material flow patterns. However, for parts with significantly different geometries (e.g., long bolts, flanged components) or materials with different thermo-mechanical characteristics (e.g., titanium alloys, high-carbon steels), the relative importance of process variables may differ substantially.

A key contribution of this work is the industrial integration of the full analytical pipeline into Moornmo’s MES, enabling real-time sensing, correlation heatmaps, predictive modeling, and AI-driven parameter recommendations. Operators can visualize MHT, DT, PT, WS, MFL, FF, monitor predicted defect rates, and adjust WS and MFL proactively, reducing dependence on expert intuition and stabilizing process variability.

Limitations include the indirect nature of FF measurement via acoustic signals and the absence of direct sensing for die wear, lubrication state, and 3D temperature distribution. As all the sensors are set up and the data is still being collected. With more data, future work will incorporate direct force sensors, thermal imaging, digital-twin simulations, real-time causal inference, and expansion to other forged components, enabling more robust, self-optimizing forging systems. Furthermore, the proposed framework demonstrates a scalable architecture applicable to a variety of forging and forming operations.

Overall, this study establishes an end-to-end, data-driven methodology for intelligent warm-forging systems, demonstrating a scalable pathway to improve product quality, reduce defect rates, and increase operational stability in industrial warm forging.
